topics.title: Goa's bakers: used to and would

learn.hook: In old Goa, you could tell the time of morning by the baker's call outside your gate!
points: 'Glimpses of India' has three travel pieces: a baker from Goa, a visit to Coorg, and tea from Assam.
In Goa, traditional bakers are called paders. The baking tradition goes back to the days of Portuguese rule, and bread is part of festivals and weddings.
The Goa piece is nostalgic: it looks back fondly at the past.
'Used to' + verb shows a past habit or state that is no longer true: 'He used to come every day.'
'Would' + verb can also show a repeated past action (not a past state): 'We would wait at the gate.' In questions and negatives, write 'use to': 'Did you use to ...?'

example.q: Passage: When Nani was a girl in Margao, the baker used to come every morning with a basket of warm bread on his head. The children would rush to the gate the moment they heard his horn, hoping for a sweet bun. Which phrases show past habits, and why?
steps: 'used to come every morning' shows something that happened regularly in the past.
'would rush to the gate' also shows a repeated past action.
Both suggest it does not happen in the same way now.
example.answer: 'used to come' and 'would rush'; both describe repeated actions in the past.

learn.reallife: Grandparents often begin stories with 'We used to ...'. Ask yours what they used to eat or play as children!

items.text: My grandfather ___ walk to school every day.
Did you ___ play gilli-danda as a child?
When we were small, every Sunday we ___ visit the bakery near the church.
There ___ be a big banyan tree here.
She didn't ___ like spicy food, but now she loves it.

games.title: Goa and grammar check
items: Traditional bakers in Goa are called paders.
The lesson uses this word for Goan bakers.
Goa's baking tradition is linked to the period of Portuguese rule.
Goa was ruled by the Portuguese for centuries.
'Would' can be used for a past state, as in 'I would have long hair.'
For past states use 'used to': 'I used to have long hair.'
'Used to' describes a past habit that is no longer true.
'I used to cycle to school' implies I no longer do.
The Goa piece in 'Glimpses of India' has a nostalgic tone.
It fondly remembers the bakers of the writer's childhood.

quiz.q: What are traditional bakers called in Goa, as described in 'Glimpses of India'?
quiz.explain: Goan bakers are known as paders.
steps: In 'Glimpses of India', Goan bakers have a special name.
They are called paders.
Answer: Paders
quiz.mistake: Picks a word for another kind of food seller

quiz.q: Goa's tradition of baking bread is linked to the rule of which European power?
quiz.explain: Goa was a Portuguese colony, and baking bread came with that period.
steps: Goa was a Portuguese colony.
Baking bread in Goa came with Portuguese rule.
Answer: The Portuguese
quiz.mistake: Assumes all colonial traditions in India are British

quiz.q: Passage: When Nani was a girl in Margao, the baker used to come every morning with a basket of warm bread on his head. The children would rush to the gate the moment they heard his horn, hoping for a sweet bun. What did the children hope for?
options: A ride on the baker's cycle
quiz.explain: The last words say they hoped for a sweet bun.
steps: The passage ends: the children rushed out 'hoping for a sweet bun'.
So they hoped for a sweet bun.
Answer: A sweet bun
quiz.mistake: Does not read to the end of the sentence

quiz.q: What does 'used to' show in 'He used to come every morning'?
options: A past habit that no longer happens
quiz.explain: 'Used to' describes a regular action in the past.
steps: 'Used to' describes a regular action in the past.
It shows a past habit that no longer happens.
Answer: A past habit that no longer happens
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'used to' (past habit) with 'be used to' (be accustomed)

quiz.q: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Did you use to play cricket in school?
Did you used to play cricket in school?
Did you using to play cricket in school?
Did you uses to play cricket in school?
quiz.explain: After 'did', the base form 'use to' is used.
steps: After 'did', the verb is always in its base form.
So: Did you use to play cricket in school?
Answer: Did you use to play cricket in school?
quiz.mistake: Keeps the -d after 'did'

quiz.q: Choose the correct word: 'Long ago, on festival days, Nani ___ bake cakes for the whole street.'
quiz.explain: 'Would' shows a repeated action in the past.
steps: The sentence is about a repeated action long ago ('on festival days').
Repeated past actions take 'would'.
Answer: would
quiz.mistake: Uses a present or future form for a past habit

quiz.q: Which sentence uses 'would' wrongly?
options: We would play in the rain every monsoon.
Every evening, Dadi would tell us stories.
I would have a dog called Tommy when I was young.
On Sundays, we would visit the market.
quiz.explain: 'Having a dog' is a past state, so 'used to have' is needed; 'would' is only for repeated actions.
steps: 'Would' is used only for repeated past actions, not past states.
Having a dog is a state, so 'I would have a dog' is wrong; it needs 'used to have'.
Answer: I would have a dog called Tommy when I was young.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that 'would' is not used for past states

quiz.q: What does 'nostalgia' mean?
options: A warm, longing feeling for the past
quiz.explain: Nostalgia is a fond, slightly sad longing for the past.
steps: Nostalgia is a feeling about the past.
It is a warm, slightly sad longing for the past.
Answer: A warm, longing feeling for the past
quiz.mistake: Guesses a meaning from the Goan setting

teach.ask: Gappu: Grandpa Bird says, 'We used to fly to the river every morning.' What does 'used to' mean? Does he still go?
teach.praise: Chirp! 'Used to' means he did it regularly in the past but doesn't now. Grandpa, tell me more!
teach.nudge: Is 'used to' about now or about the past? Does the habit still continue?

revise.summary: The Goa piece of 'Glimpses of India' fondly remembers traditional bakers called paders, a tradition from the days of Portuguese rule. We also use 'used to' and 'would' for past habits.
focus: Recall facts: paders, Portuguese rule, the nostalgic tone.
Use 'used to' for past habits or states and 'would' for repeated past actions.
Write 'use to' after 'did' in questions and negatives.
remember: 'Used to' + verb shows a past habit or state that is no longer true: 'He used to come every day.'
'Would' + verb shows a repeated past action (not a past state).
Questions and negatives: 'Did you use to ...?'
traps: Don't use 'would' for a past state: 'I used to have a dog', not 'I would have a dog'.
Don't keep the -d after 'did': 'Did you use to', not 'Did you used to'.
Don't assume Goa's baking tradition is British; it goes back to Portuguese rule.

topics.title: Coorg and Assam: degrees of comparison

learn.hook: One region smells of coffee, the other of tea. Can you guess which is which?
points: Coorg (Kodagu) is a hilly district of Karnataka, famous for coffee estates, rainforests and its brave Kodava people.
The River Kaveri rises in the hills of Coorg, and the area is popular for adventure sports like river rafting.
Assam is India's largest tea-producing state. In 'Tea from Assam', two friends, Pranjol and Rajvir, travel to a tea garden and talk about legends of how tea was discovered.
Adjectives have three degrees: positive (tall), comparative for two things (taller, more beautiful), superlative for three or more (tallest, most beautiful).
Some are irregular: good-better-best, bad-worse-worst, many/much-more-most, little-less-least.

example.q: Complete: 'Coorg's hills are ___ (green) than the plains, and the coffee there is the ___ (good) I have tasted.'
steps: Two things are compared in the first part, so use the comparative: greener.
The second part compares with everything tasted: superlative.
'Good' is irregular: good-better-best.

learn.reallife: Travel websites and brochures constantly compare: 'the coolest hill station', 'cheaper than flying'.

games.title: Which place is it?
items: paders and fresh bread
Portuguese heritage
beaches on the Arabian Sea
coffee estates
source of the River Kaveri
Kodava people
vast tea gardens
the Brahmaputra valley

quiz.q: In which state is Coorg (Kodagu)?
quiz.explain: Coorg is a district of Karnataka.
steps: Coorg (Kodagu) is a hilly district.
It is in Karnataka.
Answer: Karnataka
quiz.mistake: Picks a neighbouring southern state

quiz.q: Which river rises in the hills of Coorg?
quiz.explain: The Kaveri begins in the Coorg hills.
steps: The Kaveri begins in the hills of Coorg.
So the river is the Kaveri.
Answer: Kaveri
quiz.mistake: Picks a famous river of another region

quiz.q: Which pairing is correct?
quiz.explain: Coorg is known for coffee and Assam for tea.
steps: Coorg's hills are famous for coffee plantations.
Assam is famous for tea.
Answer: Coorg: coffee; Assam: tea
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the two drinks

quiz.q: Who are the two friends in 'Tea from Assam'?
quiz.explain: Pranjol and Rajvir travel to Assam together.
steps: In 'Tea from Assam', two friends travel to a tea estate.
They are Pranjol and Rajvir.
Answer: Pranjol and Rajvir
quiz.mistake: Recalls names from other lessons

quiz.q: According to one legend in 'Tea from Assam', how was tea discovered?
options: Leaves fell into a Chinese emperor's pot of boiling water
A farmer in Goa grew it by mistake
A trader brought it from Coorg
It was found in a river in Karnataka
quiz.explain: The legend says a few leaves dropped into the emperor's boiling water and gave it a pleasant flavour.
steps: One legend says a few leaves fell into a Chinese emperor's boiling water.
The drink tasted pleasant — that was tea.
Answer: Leaves fell into a Chinese emperor's pot of boiling water
quiz.mistake: Makes up an Indian origin for the legend

quiz.q: Choose the correct form: 'Assam is ___ than Goa.'
quiz.explain: Two places are compared, so the comparative 'bigger' is used.
steps: Two places are compared (Assam and Goa).
Comparing two takes the comparative: bigger.
Answer: bigger
quiz.mistake: Uses a superlative for two things

quiz.q: Choose the correct form: 'Of all the hill stations we visited, Madikeri was the ___.'
quiz.explain: 'Of all' compares more than two, so the superlative is needed.
steps: 'Of all the hill stations' compares more than two.
That needs the superlative: coolest.
Answer: coolest
quiz.mistake: Uses the comparative when many things are compared

quiz.q: Choose the correct form: 'This tea is good, but the tea at the estate was even ___.'
quiz.explain: 'Good' is irregular: good-better-best; comparing two teas needs 'better'.
steps: 'Good' is irregular: good – better – best.
Comparing two teas needs the comparative: better.
Answer: better
quiz.mistake: Adds -er to an irregular adjective

teach.ask: Gappu: Is Assam's tea 'more good' or 'better' than mine? When do I say 'best'?
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! Better is for comparing two, best for comparing many. 'More good' isn't a thing. Got it!
teach.nudge: Which form compares two things, and which compares three or more?

revise.summary: Coorg (Kodagu) in Karnataka is known for coffee and the Kaveri rises in its hills, while Assam is India's largest tea-producing state. We also learn the three degrees of comparison.
focus: Recall facts about Coorg and 'Tea from Assam' (Pranjol and Rajvir, the legends of tea).
Use comparative for two things and superlative for three or more.
remember: Positive (tall), comparative for two things (taller, more beautiful), superlative for three or more (tallest, most beautiful).
traps: Don't use a superlative when only two things are compared.
Don't add -er to an irregular adjective: 'better', not 'gooder'.
Don't mix up the drinks: Coorg is coffee, Assam is tea.

learn.hook: A good travel description lets your reader smell the spices without leaving the sofa.
points: A travel description says where you went and how, then paints the place with details, and ends with your overall impression.
Use sensory details: sight, sound, smell, taste and touch.
Order of adjectives: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose: 'a lovely little old red Kashmiri shawl'.
'The Trees' by Adrienne Rich shows trees moving out of a house back into the forest, suggesting that living things long to be free.
Personification gives human actions or feelings to non-human things: 'the trees stretch their roots', 'the wind whispered'.

example.q: Passage: We reached Munnar by noon. Mist curled over the rolling green tea hills, and the air smelled of cardamom. A tiny old wooden stall sold hot banana fritters that crackled in the pan. Which senses does this description use?
steps: 'Mist curled over rolling green tea hills' is what we see: sight.
'smelled of cardamom' is smell.
'crackled in the pan' is sound, and 'hot fritters' suggests taste and touch.
example.answer: Sight, smell, sound, and also taste/touch through 'hot banana fritters'.

learn.reallife: Travel bloggers and tourism boards, like those for Kerala or Meghalaya, use sensory details to attract visitors.

games.title: Order the adjectives
games.prompt: Build the noun phrase in correct order
items: a
lovely
little
red
Kashmiri
shawl

games.title: Travel writing and 'The Trees'
items: A travel description should include sensory details.
Details of sight, sound and smell bring a place alive.
'a wooden old tiny stall' follows the correct order of adjectives.
Size and age come before material: 'a tiny old wooden stall'.
'The Trees' was written by Adrienne Rich.
Adrienne Rich is the poet.
In 'The Trees', the trees move from the forest into the house.
They move out of the house into the forest.
'The river sang a lullaby' is an example of personification.
Singing is a human action given to a river.
A travel description must not contain the writer's feelings.
Personal impressions make it lively.

quiz.q: Passage: We reached Munnar by noon. Mist curled over the rolling green tea hills, and the air smelled of cardamom. A tiny old wooden stall sold hot banana fritters that crackled in the pan. Which detail appeals to the sense of smell?
quiz.explain: 'Smelled of cardamom' is about smell.
steps: The question asks for a detail of smell.
'The air smelled of cardamom' is about smell.
Answer: The air smelled of cardamom
quiz.mistake: Picks a sight or sound detail

quiz.q: Passage: We reached Munnar by noon. Mist curled over the rolling green tea hills, and the air smelled of cardamom. A tiny old wooden stall sold hot banana fritters that crackled in the pan. Which detail appeals to hearing?
options: Fritters that crackled in the pan
quiz.explain: 'Crackled' is a sound.
steps: The question asks for a detail of sound.
'Fritters that crackled in the pan' — crackling is a sound.
Answer: Fritters that crackled in the pan
quiz.mistake: Confuses sound with sight

quiz.q: Which phrase has the adjectives in the correct order?
quiz.explain: Size (tiny) comes before age (old), which comes before material (wooden).
steps: Adjective order: size → age → material.
tiny (size), old (age), wooden (material): a tiny old wooden stall.
Answer: a tiny old wooden stall
quiz.mistake: Does not know the standard adjective order

quiz.q: Which phrase is in the correct order?
options: a red little lovely Kashmiri shawl
a Kashmiri lovely red little shawl
a little lovely Kashmiri red shawl
a lovely little red Kashmiri shawl
quiz.explain: Opinion, size, colour, origin: lovely, little, red, Kashmiri.
steps: Adjective order: opinion → size → colour → origin.
lovely, little, red, Kashmiri: a lovely little red Kashmiri shawl.
Answer: a lovely little red Kashmiri shawl
quiz.mistake: Puts origin or colour before opinion

quiz.q: What makes a travel description lively?
options: Sensory details and the writer's impressions
A list of train timings only
Very long sentences with no details
quiz.explain: Details and feelings help readers picture and feel the place.
steps: Readers need to picture and feel the place.
Sensory details and the writer's impressions make a description lively.
Answer: Sensory details and the writer's impressions
quiz.mistake: Thinks facts alone make good description

quiz.q: Who wrote 'The Trees'?
quiz.explain: 'The Trees' is by Adrienne Rich.
steps: 'The Trees' is a poem in this chapter.
It was written by Adrienne Rich.
Answer: Adrienne Rich
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the poets of First Flight

quiz.q: What does 'The Trees' suggest when the trees move out into the forest?
options: Living things long to be free
quiz.explain: The trees leave the house to return to the forest, showing a desire for freedom.
steps: In the poem the trees leave the house and move out into the forest.
This shows that living things long to be free.
Answer: Living things long to be free
quiz.mistake: Reads the poem literally

quiz.q: Which line uses personification?
options: The pines were tall and green.
The wind whispered through the pines.
quiz.explain: Whispering is a human action given to the wind.
steps: Personification gives human actions to non-human things.
The wind cannot really whisper, so 'The wind whispered through the pines' is personification.
Answer: The wind whispered through the pines.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any description of nature is personification

teach.ask: Gappu: I flew to the hills today! How do I describe it so my friends can feel like they were there?
teach.praise: Tweet-tweet! I'll describe what I saw, heard and smelled, and how I felt. My friends will love it!
teach.nudge: Which senses could you describe? And did you say how you felt?

revise.summary: A travel description tells where you went, paints the place with sensory details and ends with your impression. 'The Trees' by Adrienne Rich suggests living things long to be free, and uses personification.
focus: Use sight, sound, smell, taste and touch details in description.
Put adjectives in the correct order.
Explain the message of 'The Trees' and spot personification.
remember: Order of adjectives: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose: 'a lovely little old red Kashmiri shawl'.
Personification gives human actions or feelings to non-human things: 'the wind whispered'.
traps: Don't think facts alone make a good description; add sensory details and impressions.
Don't put origin or colour before opinion or size.
Not every description of nature is personification; it needs a human action or feeling.
